data:
What Prefect is, in Kubernetes terms, and how the operator maps custom resources onto Kubernetes objects and Prefect API objects.
Prefect for Kubernetes users Work pools, workers, deployments, and flow runs, compared with Kubernetes objects. How the operator works Owned objects, syncing with Prefect, adoption, finalizers, and status conditions.

The custom resources fall into two groups, and the operator reconciles each group differently.
Group Kinds The operator writes to Workload resources PrefectServer, PrefectWorkPool The Kubernetes API: Deployments, Services, PVCs, Jobs. Prefect API resources PrefectWorkPool, PrefectWorkQueue, PrefectDeployment, PrefectAutomation The Prefect API, over HTTP. PrefectWorkPool is in both groups. It creates a work pool in Prefect and runs the pool’s workers in Kubernetes.
data.adoption#Adoption:
A Prefect object can exist before the resource that manages it. For example, Prefect creates a work queue implicitly when a deployment names one.
Resource If the object already exists PrefectWorkPool Adopts it, and sets status.adopted: true. PrefectWorkQueue Adopts it, and sets status.adopted: true. PrefectDeployment Takes it over. Prefect treats creating a deployment with an existing flow and name as an update. status.adopted is not recorded. PrefectAutomation Creates a second automation with the same name. Automation names are not unique in Prefect. The operator decides adoption on the first sync and doesn’t change it later.
data.connecting-to-prefect#Connecting to Pref:
Every resource except PrefectServer has a spec.server that says which Prefect API to use:
# A PrefectServer in the cluster. namespace defaults to the resource's own. server: name: prefect namespace: prefect # Prefect Cloud, or any Prefect server outside the cluster. server: remoteApiUrl: https://api.prefect.cloud accountId: workspaceId: apiKey: valueFrom: secretKeyRef: name: prefect-api-key key: api-key For an in-cluster server, the API URL is http://..svc.cluster.local.:4200/api, or the same with your cluster domain if it isn’t cluster.local. For a remote one, it’s remoteApiUrl with /api appended if it’s missing, then /accounts//workspaces/ when both IDs are set. The operator and the workers use the same URL. A Secret or ConfigMap holding an API key must name that URL in an annotation. See Connect to Prefect Cloud.
The dot at the end of an in-cluster host makes a resolver look up that exact name, without the search domains in /etc/resolv.conf. The dot has two other effects:
NO_PROXY entries such as .cluster.local don’t match the host. If a worker or flow run pod has HTTP_PROXY, add .svc.cluster.local., with the dot, to its NO_PROXY. Without that entry, the pod sends its API requests to the proxy in plain HTTP, with any credentials they have. The operator itself doesn’t use a proxy for an in-cluster server. Istio sidecars before Istio 1.27 don’t route the host to the Service. With strict mutual TLS, requests from a worker or flow run pod with one fail. When the operator runs outside the cluster, as it does during development, it reaches an in-cluster server through kubectl port-forward.
data.deleting-a-server#Deleting a server:
Delete a server together with the resources that use it:
kubectl delete -f server.yaml -f work-pool.yaml -f deployment.yaml A PrefectServer keeps its finalizer while a PrefectWorkPool, PrefectWorkQueue, PrefectDeployment, or PrefectAutomation names it in spec.server. That includes resources in other namespaces that the operator watches. It leaves out resources that also set remoteApiUrl, because they use that URL. The server’s Deployment and Service keep running, so those resources can still delete their objects from it. When the last one is gone, the operator removes the finalizer, and garbage collection deletes the Deployment and Service.
Deleting the server’s namespace doesn’t keep the server running. Kubernetes deletes the namespace’s Deployments, Services, and Secrets directly, so the operator removes the server’s finalizer without waiting. A resource that hasn’t deleted its object from the server by then can’t reach it. The operator removes the finalizer of a resource in that namespace, as described in Deletion, and its object stays in the server’s database. A resource in another namespace isn’t deleted, and fails to sync. If you delete it after the server’s namespace is gone, it stays in Terminating for up to an hour. With an ephemeral or SQLite server, the database is deleted with the namespace. With PostgreSQL, delete the resources before the namespace to remove their objects from Prefect.
If you delete only the server, it waits until you delete the others, with no time limit. kubectl delete blocks until then, unless you pass --wait=false. The DeletionBlocked condition names up to five of the resources, and a DependentsExist Warning event repeats its message:
kubectl get prefectserver prefect -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="DeletionBlocked")].message}' 2 resources use this server and must be deleted first: PrefectDeployment default/hello, PrefectWorkPool default/process-pool To delete the server without waiting, remove its finalizer. The resources that use it then can’t reach it, and they stay in Terminating until the operator gives up after an hour:
kubectl patch prefectserver prefect --type=merge -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}' The server waits only with background cascading deletion, which is the default for kubectl delete. With --cascade=foreground, garbage collection deletes the Deployment and Service before the server, whatever finalizers the server has. The chart’s admission policies refuse a foreground delete of a PrefectServer, even one that nothing uses.
Argo CD uses foreground deletion by default. On each Application that includes a server, set the sync option for prunes, and the finalizer for deleting the Application itself:
metadata: finalizers: - resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io/background spec: syncPolicy: syncOptions: - PrunePropagationPolicy=background Garbage collection also uses foreground deletion, for a server that has an owner reference to an object deleted that way. The policy refuses it, and the owner stays in Terminating until you delete the server yourself.
data.deletion#Deletion:
Every resource has a finalizer:
Resource Finalizer PrefectServer prefect.io/server-cleanup PrefectWorkPool prefect.io/work-pool-cleanup PrefectWorkQueue prefect.io/workqueue-cleanup PrefectDeployment prefect.io/deployment-cleanup PrefectAutomation prefect.io/automation-cleanup When you delete a Prefect API resource, the operator deletes its object in Prefect and then removes the finalizer. It leaves adopted work pools and work queues in place, because something else created them and may still depend on them. A PrefectDeployment deletes the deployment it synced, even one it took over.
If the delete in Prefect fails, the operator keeps the finalizer, records a DeleteFailed Warning event, and retries. The first retry comes after one second, and each wait after that is about twice as long, up to 30 seconds. One hour after the resource’s deletion timestamp, it removes the finalizer anyway. The event then says that the object may still exist in Prefect.
In a namespace that is being deleted, the operator doesn’t wait an hour when the delete needs an object that the namespace’s deletion already removed: the Secret or ConfigMap with the API key or auth string, or the Service of the in-cluster server. Nothing can create that object again, so after the first failed delete the operator removes the finalizer. Kubernetes doesn’t accept events in a namespace that is being deleted, so the operator’s log is the only record. It names the missing object in its deleted field.
To remove a resource without touching Prefect, remove its finalizer:
kubectl patch prefectdeployment hello --type=merge -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}' kubectl delete prefectdeployment hello
data.dependencies-between-resources#Dependenc:
A PrefectDeployment or PrefectWorkQueue that names a work pool waits until the work pool exists in Prefect. Its Synced condition is False with the reason WorkPoolNotFound, and it checks again every 30 seconds. When a PrefectWorkPool with that name first syncs, the operator reconciles the waiting resources right away.
A PrefectAutomation whose actions name a deployment waits the same way, with the reason DeploymentNotFound.
You can apply all the resources at once, in any order.
data.names-in-prefect#Names in Prefect: Resource Name of the Prefect object PrefectWorkPool metadata.name PrefectWorkQueue spec.name, in the work pool spec.workPoolName PrefectDeployment metadata.name, under the flow named in spec.deployment.entrypoint after the :, or spec.deployment.flow_name PrefectAutomation spec.name Work pool names are global within a Prefect server or workspace. Two PrefectWorkPool resources with the same name in different namespaces manage the same work pool, and each one overwrites the other’s settings.
data.objects-the-operator-creates-in-kubernet:
Resource Object Name Created when PrefectServer Deployment Always. PrefectServer Service , port 4200 named api Always. PrefectServer PersistentVolumeClaim -data spec.sqlite is set. PrefectServer Job -migration- spec.postgres is set. See Server storage. PrefectWorkPool Deployment Always. spec.workers sets its replicas. Each object has an owner reference to its resource, with controller: true. Kubernetes garbage collection deletes the objects when you delete the resource. That includes the SQLite PVC, and with it the server’s database. A PrefectServer’s objects are deleted only after its finalizer is removed. See Deleting a server.
The operator overwrites changes made directly to these objects on its next reconcile. To change them, change the resource, or patch the pod template with deploymentTemplate.
Labels on the objects:
Label On prefect.io/server: Every object a PrefectServer creates. app: prefect-server The server Deployment and its pods. prefect.io/worker: The worker Deployment and its pods. spec.deploymentLabels, spec.serviceLabels, and spec.migrationJobLabels add more.
data.status#Status:
Every resource reports conditions in status.conditions. kubectl describe shows them, along with the events the operator records.
Resource Condition Meaning Prefect API resources Synced The last sync with Prefect succeeded. When False, the reason and message say why. Prefect API resources Ready The object exists in Prefect and matches the spec. PrefectServer DeploymentReconciled, ServiceReconciled The operator created or updated the object. DeploymentReconciled is False with the reason UnsupportedVersion when spec.auth is set and the image is a Prefect release that doesn’t support it, or the reason InvalidAuth when the Secret has no valid auth string or the server’s settings set another one. PrefectServer AuthSupported True when the server’s Prefect version supports spec.auth, and False when it doesn’t. Unknown when the operator can’t tell the version of the image. Without a valid auth string, it is neither True nor Unknown. PrefectServer PersistentVolumeClaimReconciled, MigrationJobReconciled As above. The reason ends in NotRequired when the storage backend doesn’t use the object. PrefectServer DeletionBlocked The server is being deleted and waits for the resources that use it. The message names them. See Deleting a server. PrefectServer SharedStateConfigured False when more than one replica runs without Redis lease storage. See Server storage. PrefectServer, PrefectWorkPool DeploymentTemplateApplied, MigrationJobTemplateApplied The pod template patch was applied. See Pod templates. PrefectWorkPool DeploymentReconciled The operator created or updated the worker Deployment. PrefectWorkPool SettingsApplied Present only when the operator left some settings out of the worker, because they set a variable that spec.server sets, such as prefect_api_url. The message names them. Synced reasons you may see:
Reason Cause PrefectClientError The operator couldn’t build a client: the Secret or ConfigMap with the API key or auth string is missing, lacks the prefect.io/allowed-api-urls annotation, or doesn’t allow the URL. SyncError The Prefect API returned an error. The message includes it. WorkPoolNotFound, DeploymentNotFound A dependency doesn’t exist in Prefect yet. See Dependencies. ConversionError The spec couldn’t be turned into a Prefect API request, for example because of an invalid schedule. InvalidSpec The spec breaks a rule that the CRD’s validation didn’t catch, such as an automation without a trigger. BaseJobTemplateError The work pool’s base job template ConfigMap or key doesn’t exist. Recreating The object was deleted in Prefect during the sync. The next sync, one second later, creates it again.
data.syncing-with-prefect#Syncing with Prefec:
The operator syncs a Prefect API resource when any of these is true:
It has no Prefect ID in status.id yet. Its spec changed since the last sync. Its resync interval has passed since status.lastSyncTime. The resync interval is the resource’s spec.interval, or the operator’s --default-resync-interval flag when that’s unset. The default is 5 minutes, and values below 10 seconds are raised to 10 seconds. The operator adds up to 10% of random jitter so that resources don’t all sync at once.
A resync corrects drift. If someone edits a managed object in the Prefect UI, the next resync writes the spec back. If someone deletes it in Prefect, the next resync creates it again.
Some Prefect objects lose state on every update, so the operator reads the object first and skips the update when nothing changed:
Updating a deployment deletes its future scheduled runs, which Prefect then schedules again. Updating an automation resets the state of a proactive trigger.

data: Prefect schedules and runs Python workflows. This page covers the Prefect terms that the custom resources use. The Prefect docs cover the rest.
data.how-a-flow-run-reaches-a-pod#How a flow: A schedule on a deployment, or a person in the UI, creates a flow run in the server. The run is scheduled on the deployment’s work pool. A worker polling that work pool picks up the run. The worker starts the run on the pool’s infrastructure, filling in the pool’s base job template with the deployment’s jobVariables. The flow run’s process pulls the flow code, using the deployment’s pullSteps, and runs the flow. It reports state back to the server. The worker and the flow run both talk to the Prefect API over HTTP. Neither needs to reach the Kubernetes API, except for a kubernetes worker creating Jobs.
data.job-templates-and-job-variables#Job temp:
A work pool’s base job template is a JSON document with two parts. variables is a JSON schema of the settings a deployment may change, such as image or namespace. job_configuration is the infrastructure spec, with {{ variable }} placeholders. For a kubernetes pool, job_configuration holds a Job manifest.
spec.baseJobTemplate on a PrefectWorkPool picks the template:
Field Template unset The worker type’s default, which the operator reads from the Prefect server. value An inline JSON object. configMap A key in a ConfigMap in the work pool’s namespace, holding the template as a JSON string. The operator watches the ConfigMap and syncs the work pool again when it changes. patches RFC 6902 JSON patches applied to whichever template the other fields pick, including the default. For example, to give every flow run of a kubernetes pool a default memory request without writing out the whole default template:
spec: type: kubernetes baseJobTemplate: patches: - op: add path: /job_configuration/job_manifest/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources value: requests: memory: 512Mi A deployment’s spec.deployment.jobVariables fills in the variables. A deployment can change only what the template exposes as a variable.
This makes the work pool’s template the place to set limits on flow-run pods. Anyone who can write a PrefectDeployment can choose any value the template’s variables allow.
data.terms#Terms: Prefect term What it is Closest Kubernetes idea Flow A Python function decorated with @flow. The program in a container image. Flow run One execution of a flow. A Job’s pod. Server The Prefect API and UI, backed by a database. Prefect Cloud is a hosted server. The API server and etcd. Deployment A flow’s code location, default parameters, schedules, and work pool. Not a Kubernetes Deployment. A CronJob, without the pod template. Work pool A named queue of scheduled flow runs, plus a job template that describes the infrastructure for each run. A scheduler’s queue. Work queue A subdivision of a work pool with its own priority and concurrency limit. A priority class with a quota. Worker A long-running process that polls one work pool and starts each flow run on the pool’s infrastructure. A controller that turns queue entries into pods. Automation A trigger on Prefect events or metrics, and the actions it runs, such as pausing a deployment or sending a notification. An alerting rule with a webhook. The name collision matters in kubectl output. A PrefectDeployment creates a Prefect deployment through the Prefect API. It creates no Kubernetes Deployment. A PrefectServer and a PrefectWorkPool each create a Kubernetes Deployment.
data.work-pool-types#Work pool types:
spec.type on a PrefectWorkPool decides where flow runs execute.
Type Where each flow run runs What the worker needs process A subprocess in the worker’s pod. Nothing beyond its pod. Flow runs share the worker’s CPU, memory, and image. kubernetes A Kubernetes Job that the worker creates. A ServiceAccount, set with spec.serviceAccountName, that may create and watch Jobs and Pods in the namespace the job template names. For kubernetes, the operator uses the prefecthq/prefect:-python3.12-kubernetes image for the worker. The operator does not create the worker’s ServiceAccount or its RBAC. A minimal Role for a worker that runs Jobs in its own namespace:
apiVersion: v1 kind: ServiceAccount metadata: name: prefect-worker --- apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: Role metadata: name: prefect-worker rules: - apiGroups: ["batch"] resources: ["jobs"] verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete"] - apiGroups: [""] resources: ["pods", "pods/log", "events"] verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"] --- apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: RoleBinding metadata: name: prefect-worker roleRef: apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io kind: Role name: prefect-worker subjects: - kind: ServiceAccount name: prefect-worker Check the Role against the Prefect Kubernetes worker docs for the Prefect version you run.

data:
Install the operator, then run a Prefect server, a worker, and a scheduled flow in one namespace.
Install Apply the release manifest with kubectl, or install the Helm chart. Quickstart Run a server, a work pool with one worker, and a deployment that runs every minute. Upgrade What changes in each release, and what to do before you upgrade.

Each GitHub release has two manifests:
File Contents prefect-operator.yaml The CRDs, and the operator’s ServiceAccount, RBAC, and Deployment. v1.0 and later also include the admission policies. prefect-crds.yaml The CRDs only.
data.check-that-its-running#Check that it’s r: kubectl get deployment prefect-operator kubectl get crds | grep prefect.io The second command lists five CRDs: prefectautomations, prefectdeployments, prefectservers, prefectworkpools, and prefectworkqueues.
data.requirements#Requirements: Kubernetes 1.30 or later for the admission policies. CI tests the chart on the versions listed in operator-lint-and-test.yaml. Without the admission policies, see Permissions for what anyone who can write the custom resources can do.
data.uninstall#Uninstall:
Delete the custom resources first, so the operator can delete the objects it created in Prefect. Then delete the operator:
kubectl delete prefectautomations,prefectdeployments,prefectworkqueues,prefectworkpools,prefectservers --all -A kubectl delete -f https://github.com/PrefectHQ/prefect-operator/releases/download/$VERSION/prefect-operator.yaml Each PrefectServer stays up until the resources that use it are gone, so they can delete their objects from it.
If you delete the operator first, the resources keep their finalizers and stay in Terminating. See Deletion.
data.upgrade-and-downgrade#Upgrade and downgr: See Upgrade for what changes in each release, and what to do before you upgrade or after you downgrade.
data.with-helm#With Helm: helm repo add prefect-operator https://prefecthq.github.io/prefect-operator helm repo update helm install prefect-operator prefect-operator/prefect-operator \ --namespace prefect-system --create-namespace The chart’s values are listed in the chart README, which also covers verifying the chart’s signature.
data.with-kubectl#With kubectl:
VERSION=v1.0.0 kubectl apply --server-side \ -f https://github.com/PrefectHQ/prefect-operator/releases/download/$VERSION/prefect-operator.yaml The CRDs are large, so apply with --server-side. A client-side apply stores the whole object in the kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration annotation, which can exceed the 256 KiB annotation limit.
The manifest installs the operator into the default namespace. To read it before applying it:
curl -sL https://github.com/PrefectHQ/prefect-operator/releases/download/$VERSION/prefect-operator.yaml \ | grep -E '^kind:' | sort | uniq -c

data: This runs a Prefect server, a worker, and a scheduled flow in one namespace. It takes about five minutes, most of it pulling the Prefect image.
data.1-start-a-prefect-server#1. Start a Pref:
server.yaml apiVersion: prefect.io/v1 kind: PrefectServer metadata: name: prefect spec: {} kubectl apply -f server.yaml kubectl get prefectserver prefect --watch An empty spec gives an ephemeral server: its database is SQLite in an emptyDir, so it loses everything when the pod restarts. Wait for READY to become true:
NAME VERSION READY prefect 3.9.4 true The operator created a Deployment and a Service, both named prefect, and owns them:
kubectl get deployment,service -l prefect.io/server=prefect
data.2-add-a-work-pool-and-a-worker#2. Add a:
A work pool is a named queue of flow runs in Prefect. A worker is a process that polls one work pool and runs what it finds. The process type runs each flow as a subprocess of the worker, which keeps this example to one pod.
work-pool.yaml apiVersion: prefect.io/v1 kind: PrefectWorkPool metadata: name: process-pool spec: type: process server: name: prefect workers: 1 kubectl apply -f work-pool.yaml kubectl get prefectworkpool process-pool NAME TYPE VERSION READY DESIRED WORKERS READY WORKERS process-pool process 3.9.4 true 1 1
data.3-deploy-a-flow#3. Deploy a flow:
A Prefect deployment tells Prefect where a flow’s code is and when to run it. This one clones a public repository and runs hello from flows/hello_world.py every minute:
deployment.yaml apiVersion: prefect.io/v1 kind: PrefectDeployment metadata: name: hello spec: server: name: prefect workPool: name: process-pool deployment: entrypoint: flows/hello_world.py:hello pullSteps: - prefect.deployments.steps.git_clone: repository: https://github.com/PrefectHQ/examples.git branch: main parameters: name: Kubernetes schedules: - slug: every-minute cron: "* * * * *" kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml kubectl get prefectdeployment hello -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Synced")]}{"\n"}' Within a minute or two, the worker’s logs show the flow run:
kubectl logs deployment/process-pool -f
data.4-open-the-prefect-ui#4. Open the Prefec: kubectl port-forward service/prefect 4200:4200 Open http://localhost:4200. The deployment hello is under Deployments, and its runs are under Runs.
data.clean-up#Clean up: kubectl delete -f server.yaml -f work-pool.yaml -f deployment.yaml The command waits while the operator deletes the deployment and the work pool from Prefect. The PrefectServer stays up until both are gone, and then Kubernetes deletes it along with its Deployment and Service. See Deleting a server.
data.next-steps#Next steps: Keep the server’s data: Server storage. Run each flow in its own pod: set the work pool’s type to kubernetes. See Prefect for Kubernetes users. Use Prefect Cloud instead of an in-cluster server: Connect to Prefect Cloud.

data: Read the notes below for each release between yours and the new one, then upgrade the operator. Each GitHub release also lists every change it includes.
data.before-you-upgrade#Before you upgrade:
Annotate the Secrets and ConfigMaps that hold API keys. The operator reads an API key only from an object with the prefect.io/allowed-api-urls annotation, which lists the API URLs the key may be sent to. Until the object has it, a resource that uses the key has Synced False with the reason PrefectClientError. Deleting the resource keeps it in Terminating for an hour, and then leaves its object in Prefect. To list the objects that need the annotation:
kubectl get prefectworkpools,prefectworkqueues,prefectdeployments,prefectautomations -A \ -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.namespace} secret/{.spec.server.apiKey.valueFrom.secretKeyRef.name} configmap/{.spec.server.apiKey.valueFrom.configMapKeyRef.name}{"\n"}{end}' | awk '{ for (i = 2; i <= 3; i++) if ($i !~ /\/$/) print $1, $i }' | sort -u data-eng secret/prefect-api-key ml configmap/prefect-api-key Then annotate each one with the URL its resources use:
kubectl -n data-eng annotate secret/prefect-api-key \ prefect.io/allowed-api-urls=https://api.prefect.cloud/api/accounts//workspaces/ See the annotation for which URLs an entry matches.
Grant the RBAC that the admission policies check. The release manifest and the chart now install admission policies. Writing a PrefectServer or PrefectWorkPool then requires create on deployments in its namespace. Writing a PrefectWorkQueue, PrefectDeployment, or PrefectAutomation requires get on the Secret or ConfigMap that it reads the API key or auth string from. The policies check new writes only, so existing resources keep working until someone changes them. With Helm, set admissionPolicy.enabled=false to leave the policies out.
Set a version on servers and work pools that must not change. The default Prefect version is now 3.9.4. It used to be 3.9.1. The pods of a server or work pool that sets neither version nor image are replaced. An ephemeral server loses its database, and a PostgreSQL server runs its migrations. To keep the old version, set it first:
kubectl -n data-eng patch prefectserver prefect --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"version":"3.9.1"}}' Remove API settings from work pools. A work pool’s settings can’t set PREFECT_API_URL, PREFECT_API_KEY, or PREFECT_API_AUTH_STRING any more. On an existing work pool, the operator leaves them out of the worker, in any letter case, and names them in the SettingsApplied condition. The worker then uses the URL from spec.server. The CRD rejects new writes that set them. To list the work pools that set one:
kubectl get prefectworkpools -A \ -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.namespace}/{.metadata.name} {.spec.settings[*].name}{"\n"}{end}' | grep -iE ' PREFECT_API_(URL|KEY|AUTH_STRING)( |$)' Set spec.server.remoteApiUrl in place of PREFECT_API_URL, and spec.server.apiKey in place of PREFECT_API_KEY. The operator uses them too, so it must be able to reach that URL.
With rbac.operator.create=false, update the operator’s role. It needs get on secrets, or a resource that reads an API key or auth string from a Secret doesn’t sync. It also needs get on namespaces, and create and patch on events in the events.k8s.io API group. Without those two, a deleted namespace can stay in Terminating, and the operator records no events.
Run Kubernetes 1.30 or later. The policies need it, and the chart refuses to install on earlier versions.
With Argo CD, use background deletion. The policies refuse a foreground delete of a PrefectServer, and Argo CD uses foreground deletion by default. On each Application that includes a server, set the PrunePropagationPolicy=background sync option. If it has the finalizer resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io, change that to resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io/background. See Deleting a server.
With Helm, let the release take over the CRDs. The chart now upgrades the CRDs, and the first upgrade fails with an error that a CRD “exists and cannot be imported into the current release”. With Helm 3.17 or later, pass --take-ownership on that upgrade. For an earlier Helm, see the chart README. If you run more than one release of the chart in a cluster, set crds.install=false on all but one.
The chart also creates editor and viewer ClusterRoles for PrefectWorkQueue, PrefectDeployment, and PrefectAutomation, such as prefect-workqueue:editor. If a ClusterRole with one of those names already exists outside the release, the upgrade fails. With --take-ownership, or with the release manifest, it replaces that ClusterRole’s rules. To keep yours with Helm, set the chart value for that role to false, such as rbac.userRoles.prefectWorkQueue.editor.create.
Check worker and flow run pods that use an HTTP proxy or Istio. The host in an in-cluster server’s URL now ends with a dot. If the pods have HTTP_PROXY, add .svc.cluster.local., with the dot, to their NO_PROXY. Without that entry, they send API requests to the proxy in plain HTTP, including the API key or auth string. If the pods have Istio sidecars, upgrade to Istio 1.27 or later. See Connecting to Prefect.
data.downgrade#Downgrade:
v1.0 and later add the finalizer prefect.io/server-cleanup to each PrefectServer. Earlier releases don’t remove it, so after a downgrade to one of them, a deleted server stays in Terminating, and so does a namespace that has one. After you downgrade, remove the finalizer from each server:
kubectl get prefectservers -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.namespace} {.metadata.name}{"\n"}{end}' | while read -r namespace name; do kubectl -n "$namespace" patch prefectserver "$name" --type=merge -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}' done Do this after the downgrade, because a later release adds the finalizer back while it runs.
data.new#New: Server authentication: PrefectServer.spec.auth and spec.server.auth. It requires Prefect 3.6.22 or later. Pod templates: deploymentTemplate and migrationJobTemplate. Warning events when a sync or a delete fails. Editor and viewer ClusterRoles for PrefectWorkQueue, PrefectDeployment, and PrefectAutomation. See Roles for people.
data.upgrade-the-operator#Upgrade the operato:
With the release manifest, apply the new release’s manifest. It updates the CRDs too:
VERSION=v1.0.0 kubectl apply --server-side \ -f https://github.com/PrefectHQ/prefect-operator/releases/download/$VERSION/prefect-operator.yaml With Helm, find the chart version whose APP VERSION is the release, and upgrade to it:
helm repo update helm search repo prefect-operator/prefect-operator --versions | head helm upgrade prefect-operator prefect-operator/prefect-operator \ --namespace prefect-system --version
data.what-changes#What changes:
The URL of an in-cluster server ends with the cluster domain and a dot, as in http://prefect.data-eng.svc.cluster.local.:4200/api. It used to end at .svc. The worker pods of each work pool that names a server in spec.server.name are replaced once. On process work pools, that interrupts the flow runs in progress. The operator reads the domain from its pod’s DNS search domains. Set operator.clusterDomain if the log line “URLs of in-cluster Prefect servers use this cluster domain” has the wrong one.
spec.server.name and spec.server.namespace must be DNS labels, which have no upper-case letters. An existing resource with another value gets Synced False.
A PrefectServer gets the finalizer prefect.io/server-cleanup. Deleting the server waits until no resource names it in spec.server, unless its namespace is being deleted. See Deleting a server. Servers stay in Terminating if you remove the operator before them. See Uninstall.
With PostgreSQL, the operator doesn’t roll out a server whose migration Job failed. It used to roll out the server anyway. See Server storage.
When the delete in Prefect fails, the operator keeps the resource’s finalizer and retries for up to an hour, with a DeleteFailed event. It used to remove the finalizer at once, and leave the object in Prefect.
Deleting a PrefectWorkPool leaves the work pool in Prefect when the resource adopted it, which status.adopted records. Work pools that an earlier operator synced are recorded as created, so deleting them still deletes the pool. To keep one, mark it adopted first:
kubectl patch prefectworkpool --subresource=status --type=merge -p '{"status":{"adopted":true}}' remoteApiUrl must be an http or https URL with a host, and no user information, query, or fragment. An existing resource with another URL gets Synced False. The operator doesn’t connect to link-local addresses, such as 169.254.169.254.
A resource that sets both apiKey.value and apiKey.valueFrom uses valueFrom. The CRD rejects new writes that set both.
Removing a field from a PrefectDeployment schedule, such as timezone, now removes it in Prefect on the next sync.
A resource that waits for a work pool or deployment syncs as soon as the PrefectWorkPool or PrefectDeployment it names syncs. For an object created outside the operator, it checks every 30 seconds, where it used to check every 5.
The operator logs JSON at info level. It used to log console text at debug level. Set the chart values operator.logFormat: console and operator.logLevel: debug to get the old output.

data:
Steps for specific tasks.
Server storage Choose ephemeral, SQLite, or PostgreSQL storage, and add Redis for more than one replica. Require authentication Make a server require an auth string, and use it from other namespaces. Connect to Prefect Cloud Point resources at a Prefect Cloud workspace with an API key in a Secret. Pod templates Patch the pods the operator creates for servers, workers, and migration Jobs. Permissions What the operator’s ClusterRole allows, and the roles to grant your users. Troubleshooting Read conditions, events, and operator logs, and fix common failures.

data.admission-policies#Admission policies:
The chart installs three ValidatingAdmissionPolicies. Two of them close the first two rows. Writing a resource then also requires the RBAC for what the operator does with it:
Resource The requester also needs PrefectServer, PrefectWorkPool create on deployments in the resource’s namespace. PrefectWorkQueue, PrefectDeployment, PrefectAutomation get on the Secret or ConfigMap that spec.server.apiKey.valueFrom names, and on the Secret that spec.server.auth names. When a request fails a policy, the API server rejects it with a message such as:
the operator creates a Deployment from each PrefectWorkPool, so writing its spec requires permission to create Deployments in namespace data-eng The third policy refuses a foreground delete of a PrefectServer. See Deleting a server.
The first two policies don’t check a request that leaves the spec unchanged, such as the operator adding its finalizer. They check new requests only, so resources that already exist aren’t checked until someone changes them.
The policies need Kubernetes 1.30 or later. The chart value admissionPolicy.enabled controls whether the chart installs them. Without them, the prefect.io/allowed-api-urls annotation still applies.
data.roles-for-people#Roles for people:
The chart creates an editor and a viewer ClusterRole for each custom resource, for admins to bind to people. The operator doesn’t use them.
ClusterRole Grants prefect-server:editor Full access to prefectservers. prefect-server:viewer get, list, watch on prefectservers. The others are prefect-workpool, prefect-workqueue, prefect-deployment, and prefect-automation, each with :editor and :viewer. The editor roles grant only the Prefect resources, so with the admission policies enabled, also grant the permissions in the table above. For example, a team that manages its own work pools in data-eng:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: RoleBinding metadata: name: data-eng-prefect namespace: data-eng roleRef: apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io kind: ClusterRole name: prefect-workpool:editor subjects: - kind: Group name: data-eng --- apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: Role metadata: name: create-deployments namespace: data-eng rules: - apiGroups: ["apps"] resources: ["deployments"] verbs: ["create"] --- apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: RoleBinding metadata: name: data-eng-create-deployments namespace: data-eng roleRef: apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io kind: Role name: create-deployments subjects: - kind: Group name: data-eng
data.what-the-operator-can-do#What the operat:
The operator runs with a ClusterRole. Its rules are generated from the controllers and are in files/role.yaml. In every namespace it watches, it can:
create, update, and delete Deployments, Services, and PVCs create and delete Jobs read ConfigMaps, and read Secrets by name read Pods read Namespaces by name, to check whether one is being deleted create Events manage the five Prefect custom resources and their status It reads Secrets by name only, with no list or watch: the ones that a resource’s spec.server.apiKey.valueFrom or spec.server.auth names. Database and Redis passwords, and a server’s own spec.auth, are passed to pods as secretKeyRef environment variables, so the operator never reads them.
To limit it to some namespaces, set the WATCH_NAMESPACES environment variable on the operator to a comma-separated list. See Operator configuration.
data.what-writing-a-resource-lets-someone-do#:
The operator acts with its own ServiceAccount, so a resource can make it do things the person who wrote the resource can’t do directly:
Resource Lets the writer PrefectServer, PrefectWorkPool Run any container, with any ServiceAccount, in the resource’s namespace, through extraContainers, settings, serviceAccountName, and deploymentTemplate. PrefectWorkQueue, PrefectDeployment, PrefectAutomation Send the spec to Prefect with the API key or auth string in any Secret or ConfigMap in the namespace that has the prefect.io/allowed-api-urls annotation. PrefectDeployment Run flow code on the work pool’s workers, with any job settings the work pool’s base job template exposes. PrefectWorkPool, PrefectWorkQueue, PrefectDeployment, PrefectAutomation Send requests from the operator’s pod to any http or https URL in spec.server.remoteApiUrl, and read up to 4 KiB of an error response in the Synced condition. The operator can reach every in-cluster PrefectServer, so a resource in one namespace can use a server in another. To control which namespaces can use a server, require authentication on it.
The operator doesn’t connect to link-local addresses, such as the cloud instance metadata address 169.254.169.254, even through a host name that resolves to one. If the operator uses an HTTP proxy, the proxy resolves host names, so block those addresses in the proxy too. To limit which other hosts the operator can reach, apply a NetworkPolicy to its pod.

data:
Most pod settings, such as resources, node selectors, tolerations, and extra containers, have their own fields. For anything else, patch the pods the operator builds with a pod template. This one runs the server as a non-root user and gives it more time before the first readiness check:
apiVersion: prefect.io/v1 kind: PrefectServer metadata: name: prefect spec: postgres: # ... deploymentTemplate: spec: securityContext: runAsNonRoot: true runAsUser: 1001 fsGroup: 1001 containers: - name: prefect-server readinessProbe: initialDelaySeconds: 30 migrationJobTemplate: spec: securityContext: runAsNonRoot: true runAsUser: 1001 Resource Field Pods Container names PrefectServer deploymentTemplate The server Deployment prefect-server, wait-for-database (init) PrefectServer migrationJobTemplate The PostgreSQL migration Job prefect-server-migration, wait-for-database (init) PrefectWorkPool deploymentTemplate The worker Deployment prefect-worker
data.fields-the-operator-keeps#Fields the ope:
The operator applies the other fields first and the template last, so the template wins. The exception is the fields the operator depends on. It puts these back if a template overrides them:
the pod labels the Deployment selects on the api port of the prefect-server container the prefect-data volume and its mounts the environment variables the operator derives from the resource, such as the database settings and the worker’s PREFECT_API_URL, in any case. Prefect reads prefect_api_url as PREFECT_API_URL, so the operator removes a template variable with that name too. Variables from settings are not protected. When it puts a field back, the resource’s DeploymentTemplateApplied (or MigrationJobTemplateApplied) condition has the reason ProtectedFieldsIgnored. Its message lists the fields that kept the operator’s values, such as spec.containers[prefect-worker].env[PREFECT_API_URL]. The operator also records a Warning event when that list changes. Otherwise the reason is TemplateApplied.
The condition describes the pod template the operator rendered. It doesn’t confirm that running pods use it. Check DeploymentReconciled and MigrationJobReconciled for reconciliation progress and errors. The condition is removed when there is no template, or when rendering fails. On a PrefectServer, a rendering failure removes both template conditions.
data.how-the-patch-applies#How the patch appl:
A template is a partial pod template, with metadata and spec like a Deployment’s spec.template. The operator applies it as a strategic merge patch. Lists of containers are matched by name, so you can change one setting of a container without restating the rest of it. The container names above are stable. Patch directives such as $patch: delete work too.
A patch merges into what the operator built, so a probe you patch keeps the operator’s handler. To swap the handler, for example from httpGet to tcpSocket, replace the whole probe with $patch: replace:
deploymentTemplate: spec: containers: - name: prefect-server readinessProbe: $patch: replace tcpSocket: port: 4200 periodSeconds: 10 Setting httpGet: null instead works only with kubectl apply --server-side, because a client-side kubectl apply drops the null.
Lists of strings, such as args and command, are replaced, not merged. On prefect-worker, overriding args replaces the whole list, including --pool , so include every argument the worker needs.
data.invalid-templates#Invalid templates:
The template is stored without a schema, so the API server doesn’t catch a misspelled field. The operator catches it when it applies the template. It then sets DeploymentReconciled (or MigrationJobReconciled) to False with the reason InvalidPodTemplate, records a Warning event, and leaves the running pods as they are. It tries again when the template changes. A template that adds a container with the name of an existing one is rejected the same way.
The migration Job’s name comes from a hash of its spec, so changing migrationJobTemplate runs the migrations again.
data.labels-and-annotations-from-other-tools#: The operator leaves alone pod template labels and annotations that other tools add to a Deployment, such as the annotation that kubectl rollout restart sets. It records the ones it set in the Deployment’s prefect.io/pod-template-labels and prefect.io/pod-template-annotations annotations, and removes only those when they’re deleted from the template.

data:
To manage objects in a Prefect Cloud workspace, or in a Prefect server outside the cluster, give each resource a remoteApiUrl and an API key.
apiVersion: v1 kind: Secret metadata: name: prefect-api-key annotations: prefect.io/allowed-api-urls: https://api.prefect.cloud/api/accounts//workspaces/ stringData: api-key: pnu_... --- apiVersion: prefect.io/v1 kind: PrefectWorkPool metadata: name: k8s-pool spec: type: kubernetes workers: 2 serviceAccountName: prefect-worker server: remoteApiUrl: https://api.prefect.cloud accountId: workspaceId: apiKey: valueFrom: secretKeyRef: name: prefect-api-key key: api-key The account and workspace IDs are in the workspace’s URL in the Prefect Cloud UI: https://app.prefect.cloud/account//workspace/.
For a self-hosted server, set remoteApiUrl to its API URL, such as https://prefect.example.com/api, and leave out the IDs.
data.how-workers-get-the-key#How workers get:
A PrefectWorkPool worker reads the key itself, through a secretKeyRef or configMapKeyRef in the worker Deployment’s PREFECT_API_KEY variable. The operator sets the worker’s PREFECT_API_URL to the URL it checked, and the CRD rejects settings that set either variable. Prefect reads these names in any case, so the operator also leaves out a setting such as prefect_api_url and reports it in the work pool’s SettingsApplied condition.
These rules stop a work pool from sending the key to another URL by mistake. They don’t stop someone who can write the work pool on purpose, because deploymentTemplate can change the worker’s command or image. See Permissions.
If you remove a URL from the annotation later, the operator stops updating the worker Deployment. Running workers, and workers that restart, still read the key. To stop a worker from using a key, delete the PrefectWorkPool or rotate the key.
data.rules#Rules: Set apiKey.value or apiKey.valueFrom, not both. value puts the key in the resource’s spec in plain text, so prefer valueFrom. The Secret or ConfigMap must be in the resource’s namespace. With the chart’s admission policies, writing a PrefectWorkQueue, PrefectDeployment, or PrefectAutomation that names a Secret requires get on that Secret. See Permissions.
data.the-prefectioallowed-api-urls-annotation:
The operator reads an API key from a Secret or ConfigMap only if the object has the annotation prefect.io/allowed-api-urls. Its value is a comma-separated list of the Prefect API URLs that the key may be used for. The annotation stops a resource in the namespace from sending the key to a URL its owner didn’t choose.
An entry matches the resource’s API URL when:
the scheme and host, including any port, are the same, ignoring a dot at the end of the host name, and the entry’s path is the API URL’s path, or a parent of it. Entry Allows https://api.prefect.cloud/api/accounts/A/workspaces/W Workspace W only. https://api.prefect.cloud/api/accounts/A Every workspace in account A. https://api.prefect.cloud Any URL on api.prefect.cloud. The resource’s API URL is remoteApiUrl with /api appended if it’s missing, followed by /accounts//workspaces/ when both are set. For an in-cluster PrefectServer, it’s http://..svc..:4200/api. The cluster domain is usually cluster.local. The operator logs the one it uses when it starts, and the --cluster-domain flag sets it.
The operator checks the annotation each time it reads the key. Without a match, the resource’s Synced condition is False with the reason PrefectClientError, and the message names the annotation.

data:
A PrefectServer accepts API requests from anything that can reach it, unless you set spec.auth. With it, the server requires an auth string, username:password, as HTTP basic authentication on every request except its health checks. Each resource that uses the server names a Secret with the same auth string.
apiVersion: v1 kind: Secret metadata: name: prefect-auth annotations: prefect.io/allowed-api-urls: http://prefect.data-eng.svc.cluster.local:4200 stringData: auth-string: admin: --- apiVersion: prefect.io/v1 kind: PrefectServer metadata: name: prefect namespace: data-eng spec: auth: secretKeyRef: name: prefect-auth key: auth-string --- apiVersion: prefect.io/v1 kind: PrefectWorkPool metadata: name: process-pool namespace: data-eng spec: type: process workers: 1 server: name: prefect auth: secretKeyRef: name: prefect-auth key: auth-string The operator sets PREFECT_SERVER_API_AUTH_STRING on the server from the Secret, and PREFECT_API_AUTH_STRING on each work pool’s worker. A resource without spec.server.auth gets Synced False with the message API request failed with status 401.
data.flow-runs-in-kubernetes-jobs#Flow runs i:
On a work pool of type kubernetes, the operator names the auth Secret in the worker settings PREFECT_INTEGRATIONS_KUBERNETES_WORKER_API_AUTH_STRING_SECRET_NAME and ..._SECRET_KEY. Each Job then reads PREFECT_API_AUTH_STRING from the Secret. This requires prefect-kubernetes 0.6.3 or later in the worker’s image, which the Prefect 3.4.10 and later images have. An earlier worker puts the auth string in the Job’s manifest.
The Secret must exist in the namespace the Jobs run in, or their pods don’t start. Prefect’s default base job template runs Jobs in the default namespace. Set namespace in the work pool’s base job template to the work pool’s namespace, or copy the Secret to the namespace you use.
To pass the auth string in the Job’s manifest as plain text instead, set the first setting to an empty string. Anyone who can view the Jobs or pods can then read it:
spec: settings: - name: PREFECT_INTEGRATIONS_KUBERNETES_WORKER_API_AUTH_STRING_SECRET_NAME value: "" Flow code can read the auth string either way.
data.flow-runs-in-other-work-pools#Flow runs: The operator sets no such settings for other types of work pool. A worker passes the auth string to the flow runs it starts in its own way. For example, a Docker worker puts it in the container’s environment, where anyone who can inspect the container can read it. Before you use spec.server.auth with another type, see Prefect’s documentation for its worker.
data.prefect-version#Prefect version:
spec.auth requires Prefect 3.6.22 or later. Earlier servers ignore the auth string, or don’t check it on every request. When the image is a prefecthq/prefect release before 3.6.22, the operator doesn’t change the server’s Deployment, and sets DeploymentReconciled to False with the reason UnsupportedVersion. A server that already runs keeps running, without auth.
The operator can’t tell the version of other images, of tags such as 3-latest and 3.6-python3.12, or of an image with a digest. It deploys them, and sets the server’s AuthSupported condition to Unknown. The condition is absent while the server’s version is supported or unknown and its Secret or settings are invalid. To get the version of a running server:
kubectl -n data-eng exec deployment/prefect -- prefect --version
data.rules#Rules: The operator sends the auth string only to an API URL that the Secret’s prefect.io/allowed-api-urls annotation lists, and doesn’t follow redirects. See the annotation. secretKeyRef.optional must not be true. The auth string must be ASCII, have a username and a password, and not start or end with whitespace, such as a newline. Otherwise, or without the Secret, the operator doesn’t change the server’s Deployment, sets DeploymentReconciled to False with the reason InvalidAuth, and retries. The server’s settings must not set PREFECT_SERVER_API_AUTH_STRING. To move an auth string from settings to spec.auth, remove the setting in the same change. Prefect also reads the name in another case, such as prefect_server_api_auth_string. If settings sets that, the operator sets the same InvalidAuth condition until you remove it. The operator doesn’t watch the Secret. If you empty the key later, the server runs with an empty auth string from its next restart. Set spec.server.apiKey or spec.server.auth, not both. The operator sends the auth string over plain HTTP to an in-cluster server. If your pod network isn’t encrypted, for example by a service mesh with mutual TLS, other workloads on the network path can read it. With the chart’s admission policies, writing a PrefectWorkQueue, PrefectDeployment, or PrefectAutomation that names an auth Secret requires get on that Secret. See Permissions. To change the auth string, update every copy of the Secret. The server and workers read it when their pods start, so restart them: kubectl rollout restart deployment/prefect deployment/process-pool.
data.turn-it-on-for-a-running-server#Turn it:
A server without auth ignores the auth string, so set it on the clients first:
Create the Secret in the namespace of the server. Create it in the namespace of each resource that uses the server too, with the prefect.io/allowed-api-urls annotation, and in the namespace that the flow run Jobs of kubernetes work pools run in. Set spec.server.auth on each of those resources. The operator replaces the workers, which then send the auth string. On process work pools, that interrupts the flow runs in progress. Set the auth string on other clients too, such as workers you run yourself, scripts, and CI jobs. Wait for flow runs that started before step 2 to finish. They don’t have the auth string, and their API requests get a 401 after the next step. Set spec.auth on the server. Check that AuthSupported is True, and that the new server pod is ready.
data.use-a-server-from-another-namespace#Use:
A resource reads the auth string from a Secret in its own namespace. To let resources in another namespace use the server, copy the Secret there. Copy the prefect.io/allowed-api-urls annotation too, which must list the server’s in-cluster URL:
apiVersion: v1 kind: Secret metadata: name: prefect-auth namespace: ml annotations: prefect.io/allowed-api-urls: http://prefect.data-eng.svc.cluster.local:4200 stringData: auth-string: admin: Resources in ml then set spec.server.namespace: data-eng and spec.server.auth as above.
data.when-to-turn-it-on#When to turn it on:
If you isolate namespaces with NetworkPolicy, set spec.auth on every server. Otherwise the operator can reach the server on behalf of a resource in any namespace it watches. A resource can name the server in spec.server.name and spec.server.namespace, or with its Service URL in remoteApiUrl.
Without NetworkPolicy, any pod in the cluster can already call a server that has no auth.

data:
A PrefectServer stores its state in a database. Set at most one of spec.ephemeral, spec.sqlite, and spec.postgres. With none set, the server is ephemeral.
Backend Database Survives a pod restart Replicas Deployment strategy ephemeral SQLite in an emptyDir No 1 RollingUpdate sqlite SQLite on a PVC Yes 1 Recreate postgres An external PostgreSQL Yes spec.replicas, default 1 RollingUpdate
data.ephemeral#Ephemeral: apiVersion: prefect.io/v1 kind: PrefectServer metadata: name: prefect spec: ephemeral: {} Use it for trying things out and for tests. The server creates its schema on start.
data.more-than-one-replica#More than one repl:
spec: replicas: 3 postgres: # ... redis: host: redis.databases.svc port: 6379 leaseStorage: true The CRD rejects replicas above 1 unless postgres is set and sqlite is not.
Prefect keeps concurrency limit leases in each replica’s memory by default. With more than one replica, each replica enforces limits on its own, so the cluster-wide limit is not enforced. leaseStorage: true stores leases in Redis. It needs a Prefect image whose prefect-redis package includes the lease_storage module. Without it, the server’s SharedStateConfigured condition is False with the reason InMemoryLeaseStorage.
data.postgresql#PostgreSQL:
apiVersion: prefect.io/v1 kind: PrefectServer metadata: name: prefect spec: postgres: host: postgres.databases.svc port: 5432 database: prefect userFrom: secretKeyRef: name: prefect-db key: username passwordFrom: secretKeyRef: name: prefect-db key: password Each connection setting (host, port, user, password, database) has a ...From variant that takes an EnvVarSource, so any of them can come from a Secret or ConfigMap. The operator passes them to the server as PREFECT_API_DATABASE_* environment variables.
The operator runs schema migrations in a Job before it rolls out the server:
It creates a Job named -migration-, where the hash is of the Job’s spec. The Job runs prefect server database upgrade --yes. It checks the Job every 20 seconds. Until the Job completes, it doesn’t create or update the server Deployment, and MigrationJobReconciled is False. When the Job completes, it rolls out the Deployment. Changing the image, the database settings, or migrationJobTemplate changes the hash and runs a new Job. A failed Job holds the rollout, and the condition message includes the Job’s failure message. Kubernetes deletes the Job one hour after it finishes, through ttlSecondsAfterFinished. The next reconcile then creates it again. The migrations are safe to run again.
Both the Job and the server pods have an init container, wait-for-database, that runs pg_isready until the database accepts connections. It uses postgres:16-alpine unless you set spec.postgres.waitForDatabaseImage.
data.redis#Redis:
Set spec.redis to use Redis for the server’s messaging broker and cache:
spec: postgres: # ... redis: host: redis.databases.svc port: 6379 passwordFrom: secretKeyRef: name: prefect-redis key: password The Prefect image must include the prefect-redis package.
data.sqlite#SQLite:
apiVersion: prefect.io/v1 kind: PrefectServer metadata: name: prefect spec: sqlite: storageClassName: standard size: 1Gi The operator creates a ReadWriteOnce PVC named -data and mounts it at /var/lib/prefect/. The Deployment uses the Recreate strategy, because two pods can’t share the volume.
The PVC has an owner reference to the PrefectServer. Deleting the PrefectServer deletes the PVC, and the database with it, unless the StorageClass’s reclaim policy is Retain.

data:
Start with the resource’s conditions and events, then the operator’s logs:
kubectl describe prefectdeployment hello kubectl logs deployment/prefect-operator -n prefect-system The tables of condition types and Synced reasons are in How the operator works.
data.a-prefectserver-is-stuck-in-terminating#:
The server waits until no resource names it in spec.server, with no time limit. Its DeletionBlocked condition says which resources those are:
kubectl get prefectserver prefect -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="DeletionBlocked")].message}' 1 resource uses this server and must be deleted first: PrefectWorkPool default/process-pool Delete those resources. The operator deletes the server after the last one is gone. See Deleting a server.
data.a-resource-is-stuck-in-terminating#A res:
The operator couldn’t delete the object in Prefect and is retrying. Look for DeleteFailed events:
kubectl get events --field-selector reason=DeleteFailed The operator gives up and removes the finalizer one hour after the deletion started. When the resource’s namespace is being deleted and the Secret, ConfigMap, or server Service that the delete needs is gone, it gives up after the first failed delete. To remove the finalizer sooner, and leave the object in Prefect, see Deletion.
If the operator isn’t running, nothing removes the finalizer. Start the operator again, or remove the finalizer by hand.
data.deleting-a-prefectserver-is-refused#Dele:
ValidatingAdmissionPolicy 'prefect-operator-server-deletion' with binding 'prefect-operator-server-deletion' denied request: foreground deletion deletes a PrefectServer's Deployment and Service before the resources that use the server can delete their objects from it; ... The chart’s admission policies refuse foreground deletes of servers. Delete the server without --cascade=foreground. If Argo CD’s prune fails with this message, set the PrunePropagationPolicy=background sync option on the Application.
If deleting an Argo CD Application fails with it, delete the server with kubectl delete prefectserver, and Argo CD finishes deleting the rest. Kubernetes doesn’t allow a new finalizer on the Application once its deletion has started, so change the finalizer of other Applications that include a server beforehand. See Deleting a server.
data.flow-run-pods-have-createcontainerconfig: A flow run on a kubernetes work pool with spec.server.auth reads the auth string from a Secret, which must exist in the namespace its Job runs in. See Flow runs in Kubernetes Jobs.
data.synced-is-false-with-prefectclienterror#:
The operator couldn’t read the API key or auth string. The message says which of these it is:
The Secret or ConfigMap doesn’t exist in the resource’s namespace. It doesn’t have the prefect.io/allowed-api-urls annotation. The annotation doesn’t list the resource’s API URL. The message includes the URL the operator computed. Compare it with the annotation, as described in Connect to Prefect Cloud.
data.synced-is-false-with-status-401#Synced i: The server requires an auth string, and the resource doesn’t send it or sends the wrong one. Set spec.server.auth to a Secret with the server’s auth string. See Require authentication.
data.synced-is-false-with-workpoolnotfound#Sy: The work pool the resource names doesn’t exist in Prefect yet. If a PrefectWorkPool creates it, check that resource’s Synced condition. The names must match exactly, and work pool names are global to the Prefect server or workspace, not per namespace.
data.the-server-rollout-doesnt-start#The serv:
With PostgreSQL, the operator waits for the migration Job to complete before it updates the server Deployment. Check the MigrationJobReconciled condition and the Job’s pods:
kubectl get jobs -l prefect.io/server= kubectl logs job/-migration- -c wait-for-database kubectl logs job/-migration- -c prefect-server-migration A Job stuck in wait-for-database can’t reach the database host.
data.the-worker-pods-arent-ready#The worker p:
The worker serves its health check on port 8080 at /health, and the liveness probe starts after 120 seconds. Check its logs:
kubectl logs deployment/ -c prefect-worker Common causes are a wrong PREFECT_API_URL, which the operator derives from spec.server, and a kubernetes worker whose ServiceAccount can’t create Jobs.

data: API reference Every field of the five custom resources. Operator configuration Command-line flags, environment variables, and Helm values.

All five kinds are in the API group prefect.io, version v1, and are namespaced.
Kind Plural Short name Field reference PrefectServer prefectservers ps PrefectServer.md PrefectWorkPool prefectworkpools pwp PrefectWorkPool.md PrefectWorkQueue prefectworkqueues PrefectWorkQueue.md PrefectDeployment prefectdeployments PrefectDeployment.md PrefectAutomation prefectautomations PrefectAutomation.md The field descriptions come from the CRD schemas, so kubectl explain shows the same text for the version installed in your cluster:
kubectl explain prefectworkpool.spec kubectl explain prefectserver.spec.postgres --recursive
data.printer-columns#Printer columns:
kubectl get shows these columns:
Kind Columns PrefectServer VERSION, READY PrefectWorkPool TYPE, VERSION, READY, DESIRED WORKERS, READY WORKERS

data.environment-variables#Environment variab: Variable Description WATCH_NAMESPACES A comma-separated list of namespaces to watch. When it’s unset, the operator watches all namespaces. WATCH_NAMESPACES limits what the operator reconciles. It doesn’t limit its RBAC, which is a ClusterRole in both the release manifest and the chart.
data.flags#Flags: Flag Default Description --default-resync-interval 5m How often to re-check each Prefect API resource against Prefect, unless the resource sets spec.interval. --reconcile-timeout 2m How long one reconcile may run before its context is canceled and it is retried. 0 means no limit. --cluster-domain The DNS domain of the cluster, which the URLs of in-cluster Prefect servers end with. When empty, the operator reads it from the search domains in /etc/resolv.conf, and uses cluster.local if they do not include it. --leader-elect false Elect a leader, so that only one replica reconciles. The release manifest and the chart set it. The lease is named fd9f6399.prefect.io. --metrics-bind-address :8080 The address of the Prometheus metrics endpoint. --health-probe-bind-address :8081 The address of /healthz and /readyz. --enable-http2 false Serve the metrics endpoint over HTTP/2. --zap-log-level info debug, info, error, or an integer above 0 for more verbose debug logs. --zap-encoder json json or console.
data.helm-values#Helm values:
The chart sets the flags from these values:
Value Flag operator.defaultResyncInterval --default-resync-interval operator.clusterDomain --cluster-domain operator.logLevel --zap-log-level operator.logFormat --zap-encoder Set environment variables such as WATCH_NAMESPACES with operator.extraEnvVars:
operator: extraEnvVars: - name: WATCH_NAMESPACES value: data-eng,analytics The chart README lists every value.
data.without-helm#Without Helm:
Edit the operator Deployment’s args and env in the release manifest before applying it, or patch it afterwards:
kubectl set env deployment/prefect-operator WATCH_NAMESPACES=data-eng,analytics
